stem: A 40-year-old man has autoimmune gastritis that destroys the glands of his gastric body. Loss of his chief-cell secretion most directly reduces the initial digestion of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.misconception: Starch digestion is being assigned to the stomach.
options.explanation: Starch digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase and is completed by pancreatic amylase and brush-border enzymes, not by pepsin.

options.label: B
options.misconception: None; pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach.
options.explanation: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which acid converts to pepsin; pepsin starts the enzymatic digestion of proteins, so losing chief cells removes this first step.

options.label: C
options.misconception: Nucleic-acid breakdown is being assigned to the stomach.
options.explanation: Nucleic acids are digested by pancreatic nucleases and brush-border enzymes in the small intestine, well downstream of pepsin's action.

options.label: D
options.misconception: Fat digestion is being assigned to a gastric protease.
options.explanation: Triglyceride digestion depends mainly on pancreatic lipase with bile-salt emulsification in the small intestine; pepsin does not act on lipids.

options.label: E
options.misconception: Sugar digestion is being assigned to a protease.
options.explanation: Disaccharides are split by brush-border enzymes such as lactase and sucrase on the microvilli of the small intestine, not by pepsinogen or pepsin.

context: Learning objective: link chief cells to protein digestion. Chief cells of the gastric glands secrete pepsinogen; HCl from parietal cells converts it to active pepsin, which begins protein digestion. Carbohydrate, lipid, nucleic-acid, and disaccharide digestion are handled downstream by pancreatic and brush-border enzymes.
imageCaption: Gastric phases cephalic/gastric/intestinal; parietal (HCl+IF), chief (pepsinogen), G cell (gastrin).
